summary: Creates a registry for Mandatory Access Control security label formats. As MAC systems become more widely deployed, protocols need flexible ways to carry labels, and this registry lets different formats be named and referenced consistently.

eli5.summary: Documents sometimes need stickers like secret or public. This makes a list of sticker styles so everyone can refer to them by name.

subtitle: A registry that lets many different security label formats share one numbered list instead of forcing a single format.

tldr.problem: Mandatory Access Control systems use security labels that differ so much that no single label format could suit them all, yet protocols such as NFS need to carry labels between systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates the IANA 'Security Label Format Selection Registry', which maps an integer Label Format Specifier (0 to 65535) to a published document describing a label format.
tldr.outcome: Protocols can name the label format they use without the IETF picking one model; new formats are added through the Specification Required policy with Designated Expert review.

today: RFC 7569 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The registry it creates is the place where label format specifiers are assigned.

sections.title: Why a Registry Instead of One Label Format
sections.content:
As security labels spread into mainstream operating systems, systems need to send labels to each other. In a client and server setting, the client request acts as a subject trying to access an object on the server. But systems implement different Mandatory Access Control (MAC) models that typically share no common ground, and attempts at one common label format have been unsuccessful.

One idea is a single format that is the union of every known MAC model. The RFC rejects it: many models would have blank fields, or implementations would ignore many of the values present, and the interaction of fields from different models would never be clearly specified. Adding new models would also be unduly difficult.

Instead, the RFC creates a registry of label format specifications so that several MAC mechanisms and label formats can co-exist in a network. The first user is the Network File System (NFS), but other IETF protocols may reference it later.
sections.eli5: Trying to make one sticker that works for everybody would be a mess. So instead, there is a list of sticker styles, and each thing says which style it uses.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
A Label Format Specifier is an identifier the client uses to establish the syntactic format of a security label and the meaning of its components. A Label Format Specification is a reference to a stable, public document that defines the label format.

The RFC also defines the words it relies on. Multi-Level Security (MLS) is a traditional model where subjects get a security level such as Unclassified, Secret or Top Secret, and objects get labels that decide which subjects may access them. An object is a passive resource to protect, such as a file, directory, pipe or socket. A subject is an active entity, usually a process, user or client, requesting access to an object.
sections.eli5: A subject is the person asking to open the box, and an object is the box. The label on the box says who is allowed to open it.

sections.title: Existing Label Formats
sections.content:
The RFC lists four formats already in use and registered at the start.

  • IPSO Basic Security Option (BSO), defined in RFC 1108. IANA assigned IPv4 Option 130 to it. The RFC says IPSO is the only IPv4 sensitivity label option implemented in commercial IP routers.
  • CIPSO, documented in an expired draft and in FIPS 188. IANA assigned IPv4 option number 134, and CIPSO is defined only as an IPv4 option, never for IPv6.
  • CALIPSO, specified in RFC 5570 for IPv6. It is a direct derivative of the IPv4 'Son of IPSO' (SIPSO) and is not derived from CIPSO.
  • FLASK, the Flux Advanced Security Kernel, an architecture for flexible support of security policies.
sections.eli5: Some sticker styles already exist, made by different groups for different kinds of mail. The list starts by writing these down.

sections.title: The Security Label Format Selection Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a registry with four fields. The Label Format Specifier is an integer in the range 0..65535. The Label Description is a human-readable ASCII string of at most 128 bytes. The Status is a short ASCII string, normally 'active', or 'obsoleted by entry NNN' for an obsolete entry. The Label Format Specification points to a stable, public document.

The initial assignments reserve 0, set aside 1 to 127 for Private Use and 128 to 255 for Experimental Use, and give 256 to CIPSO (tag type #1), 257 to CALIPSO, 258 to the FLASK Security Context and 259 to IPSO. The range 260 to 65535 is available for IANA assignment.
sections.eli5: Each sticker style gets a number. Some numbers are saved for practice or private use, and the rest are handed out one at a time.

sections.title: Adding, Obsoleting and Modifying Entries
sections.content:
A new entry needs a label format specification document. IANA applies the Specification Required policy from RFC 5226, so a published specification and a Designated Expert review are both needed. If the specification is an RFC, its IANA Considerations section should reference the registry and request a new entry.

The Designated Expert checks that the specification gives enough meaning for object and subject labels to enforce the MAC model and policy administration, that a correct and complete protocol implementation can process and enforce the labels, and that syntax and semantics are clearly defined to reduce interoperability problems.

If a label format changes later, a new selector must be requested and the new specification should say which old assignment it obsoletes. The old entry's status becomes 'obsoleted by' the new number. Changing an entry's description or specification also uses Specification Required: if the change obsoletes the specifier the obsoleting process applies, and otherwise the reviewer approves the update.
sections.eli5: To add a new style, you must write down exactly how it works and an expert checks it. If a style changes, it gets a new number and the old one is marked as replaced.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no security considerations for associating a Label Format Specifier with a document that describes a label's syntax and format. The documents referenced by each registry entry are expected to state the security considerations of the label mechanism they specify.
sections.eli5: The list only says which sticker style is which. Each style's own instructions explain how to keep things safe.
